nodes.description: For proven, highly probable, or possible congenital syphilis (scenarios 1 and 2): aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IV every 12 hours in the first 7 days of life and every 8 hours thereafter, for 10 days. nodes.description: The pregnant woman receives the benzathine penicillin G regimen for her stage of syphilis. This is treatment of an active maternal (and often fetal) infection, so it is bound as pharmacotherapy and categorized as therapeutic; its preventive effect on the newborn is the outcome. It prevents congenital syphilis in about 98% of treated pregnancies. Treatment adequate to prevent congenital syphilis must begin at least 30 days before delivery. Failure is most likely with maternal secondary syphilis and with sonographic signs of fetal infection. For primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis a second dose a week after the first can be given. Missed doses more than 9 days apart are not acceptable for late latent syphilis. No alternative to penicillin is proven in pregnancy: a penicillin-allergic woman is desensitized. Erythromycin and azithromycin do not reliably cure the mother or treat the fetus, tetracycline and doxycycline are avoided in the second and third trimesters, and data are insufficient for ceftriaxone. Treatment in the second half of pregnancy can precipitate a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, with preterm labor, fetal distress, and rarely stillbirth, which should not delay treatment.

evidence.reference_title: A case series of 130 neonates with congenital syphilis: preterm neonates had more clinical evidences of infection than term neonates.
evidence.snippet: Compared with term neonates with CS, preterm ones were more likely to have characteristic skin rash (36.2 vs. 9.7%, p < 0.001), hepatomegaly (51.7 vs. 25%, p = 0.02), splenomegaly (32.8 vs. 15.4%, p = 0.02), PRP titer ≥1:8 (96.6 vs. 70.8%, p < 0.001), thrombocytopenia (43.1 vs. 23.6%, p = 0.018), elevated CRP (65.5 vs. 36.5%, p = 0.002), and abnormal long bone X-ray results (94.6 vs. 68.1%, p < 0.001).

nodes.description: T. pallidum attaches to and crosses the placenta. The organism lacks toxins but binds fibronectin and laminin, which helps it attach to endothelium and leave blood vessels. The adhesin Tp0751 (pallilysin) binds endothelial cells through the 67-kDa laminin receptor (LamR) and is implicated in crossing vascular, placental and blood-brain barriers, and a surface lipoprotein (Tp0954) mediates attachment to placental cell lines. Both were shown in cultured cells, not in human placenta. Treponemes are visible in the placenta in many cases, with increased numbers of Hofbauer cells, the placental macrophages.
